Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations.

source_records.title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons
source_records.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations.

papers.title: Risk Communication in a Post-Pandemic World: Lessons from the 2026 Andes Virus Outbreak
papers.abstract: In May 2026, a hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship triggered public alarm disproportionate to its actual scale, despite the rapid diagnosis, clear WHO and ECDC guidance, and swift containment within three months. This commentary asks why outbreaks that health authorities handle correctly can still produce pandemic-level panic. Drawing on media framing research and the Hondius case itself, there seem to be two forces at work. One is news coverage that foregrounds alarming questions while burying expert reassurances. The second one is that post-pandemic public has learnt to distrust reassurance after Covid, when authorities failed to convey that guidance would evolve. This piece contends that clear, accurate and timely statements from health authorities are no longer sufficient on their own and proposes three practices going forward. Recommendations involve naming and directly addressing alarming narratives early, treating community trust as infrastructure built before a crisis rather than during one, and engaging with social media conversations directly rather than relying solely on content removal. Since it was small and well controlled, this outbreak offers a low-cost opportunity to test these practices before a larger outbreak makes the same communication gap far more costly.

analysis_zh.background: 2026年安第斯病毒在MV Hondius邮轮上的疫情尽管诊断迅速、已被控制,却引发了公众的过度恐慌 (A1)。

analysis_zh.current_state: 媒体倾向于突出惊恐叙事而掩盖专家的安抚信息,公众如今不信任不断变化的指导 (A4)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 仅有明确、及时的声明已不足以遏制恐慌,暴露出疫情后重建信任的缺口 (A5)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 建议在未来低成本疫情中测试三项做法——提前命名惊恐叙事、危机前的信任基础设施建设以及主动的社交媒体参与 (A7)。

Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness. Hantaviruses are part of the family Hantaviridae, which comprises eight genera. Among them, viruses associated with human disease belong to the genus Orthohantavirus. Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses whose genome consists of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments encoding the nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoproteins Gn/Gc, and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively. The two major clinical diseases caused by orthohantaviruses are haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). HFRS is mainly caused by Asian and European orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava virus, and primarily affects the kidneys. In contrast, HPS/HCPS is caused by several American orthohantaviruses, including Orthohantavirus sinnonbrenense (Sin Nombre virus; SNV) and Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus; ANDV), and is characterised by severe respiratory disease, pulmonary oedema, and cardiovascular compromise. Importantly, ANDV-associated HPS is characterised by high case-fatality rates, with mortality estimates in Chile and Argentina ranging from approximately 21% to 50%. Orthohantavirus infection is primarily acquired by inhaling aerosolised particles contaminated with the urine, saliva, or faeces of infected rodents, although transmission may also occur through direct contact with contaminated materials or rodent bites. While most orthohantaviruses are transmitted exclusively from rodents to humans, ANDV is unique among orthohantaviruses for its demonstrated capacity for person-to-person transmission, particularly during close, prolonged contact with symptomatic individuals. Although sustained community transmission has not been demonstrated, ANDV remains the only orthohantavirus for which person-to-person transmission has been consistently documented, predominantly among close household or intimate contacts. On 4 May 2026, an international cluster of ANDV infections was identified among passengers travelling aboard the M/V Hondius following its departure from Ushuaia, Argentina. The event prompted a multinational public health response involving case isolation, quarantine, surveillance, contact tracing, and genomic investigation. The WHO declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026, with 13 cases reported, including 3 fatalities. The M/V Hondius cluster therefore provides an important contemporary example of ANDV’s epidemic potential. Could ANDV cause a future pandemic? Despite documented person-to-person transmission associated with the M/V Hondius cluster, current epidemiological and genomic evidence indicates that the likelihood of this outbreak progressing to sustained epidemic or pandemic transmission was exceedingly low. Prompt implementation of public health interventions, including quarantine measures and active surveillance of individuals aboard the vessel, facilitated the early identification and isolation of suspected cases. Furthermore, genomic analyses revealed remarkably limited viral diversity among sequenced cases from the M/V Hondius cluster, with identical S and M segment sequences and only two synonymous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) detected within the L segment, one in case 5 and another in case 7. Importantly, no evidence of amino acid changes associated with enhanced transmissibility or sustained human-to-human spread was identified. In contrast, the outbreak sequences showed approximately 98.7% nucleotide identity across all three genome segments with ANDV sequences identified in Argentina in 1997 and 2018, indicating considerably greater divergence from these historical reference sequences. Furthermore, the reported positive cases fell within the incubation period of nine to 45 days for ANDV, suggesting that the cluster may have originated from a limited zoonotic exposure event, potentially followed by restricted secondary transmission, and is unlikely to develop into an epidemic or a pandemic event. However, given that ANDV has historically caused multiple outbreaks, it is important to highlight the conditions that could enable localised ANDV outbreaks to evolve and escalate into larger epidemics, and potentially, under exceptional circumstances, into a pandemic threat among human populations, as illustrated in Figure. Potential drivers of Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak escalation and pandemic emergence. ANDV is maintained in rodent reservoirs, primarily the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), and is transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta. Unlike other orthohantaviruses, ANDV can also undergo limited person-to-person transmission, although sustained community transmission has not been documented. The graphical abstract highlights three factors that could contribute to outbreak escalation: (i) viral evolution through mutation, reassortment, and host adaptation; (ii) environmental and ecological changes that increase rodent abundance and spillover risk; and (iii) expansion of reservoir host range through host switching and reservoir diversification. Under favourable ecological and evolutionary conditions, these processes could increase the scale, frequency, geographic distribution, or transmission potential of future outbreaks, underscoring the importance of continued surveillance, preparedness, and the development of effective diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. Illustration created with BioRender.com. First - The acquisition of beneficial mutations may facilitate adaptation to human hosts. Genetic variation arising during viral replication could theoretically influence viral fitness, host range, or transmission efficiency under selective pressures. Orthohantaviruses replicate using an error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with evolutionary rates estimated at approximately 10−2-10−4 substitutions per site per year, consistent with rates reported for other RNA viruses. However, the relationship between genomic variation and altered transmissibility in ANDV remains incompletely understood, and no specific adaptive mutations have yet been conclusively associated with sustained human-to-human transmission. Previous studies have shown that ANDV strains from rodent and human hosts can produce markedly different outcomes in the Syrian hamster model. Notably, a Chilean human isolate (CHI-7913), recovered from a fatal HPS case, acquired only a single non-synonymous mutation after 25 serial passages in hamsters and remained non-pathogenic, indicating relative genomic stability. In contrast, the rodent-derived isolate Chile-9717869 causes uniformly lethal disease despite differing by 23 amino acids from CHI-7913. Although these findings suggest a degree of genomic stability, they do not necessarily preclude adaptation. One possible explanation is that the CHI-7913 isolate had already undergone host-specific adaptation following zoonotic transmission to humans, thereby enhancing fitness in human cells while reducing replication efficiency and pathogenicity in the Syrian hamster model. Collectively, these observations indicate that relatively few genetic changes can substantially alter host adaptation and disease phenotype in ANDV, while the molecular determinants governing virulence and transmissibility remain incompletely understood. Several biological mechanisms may contribute to these processes, including alterations in receptor usage, interferon antagonism, and genome reassortment. Pathogenic orthohantaviruses utilise β3 integrins, protocadherin-1, and other endothelium-associated receptors for host-cell entry, and mutations affecting glycoprotein-receptor interactions could alter host permissiveness and enhance adaptation to humans. In addition, the ability of orthohantaviruses to suppress interferon signalling contributes to reservoir persistence and may influence pathogenicity across different hosts. Importantly, the segmented orthohantavirus genome permits genetic reassortment during co-infection, potentially generating novel phenotypic combinations with altered virulence, transmissibility, or host range. Although reassortment appears less frequent than in other members of the order Bunyavirales (e.g. orthobunyaviruses) and influenza viruses, it remains an important mechanism contributing to long-term evolutionary adaptation and host expansion. Second - An increase in rodent reservoir populations driven by environmental and ecological changes may amplify the risk of zoonotic spillover. Environmental disruption is a well-recognised determinant of orthohantavirus emergence and transmission dynamics. Climatic oscillations, including El Niño-associated rainfall patterns, can substantially increase rodent abundance and population density, thereby elevating opportunities for human exposure, as previously documented during Sin Nombre virus (SNV) outbreaks in North America. In South America, deforestation, agricultural expansion, urban encroachment into rural and forested ecosystems, and biodiversity disturbance may similarly intensify contact between humans and ANDV reservoir hosts. In parallel, globalisation and expanding transportation networks have facilitated the international dissemination of rodent-associated orthohantaviruses, as illustrated by the spread of Seoul virus (SEOV) through maritime trade and the pet rat industry. Collectively, these ecological and anthropogenic pressures may increase the frequency of spillover events and the geographic distribution of orthohantavirus exposure. However, there is currently no evidence that such conditions alone are sufficient to drive sustained human-to-human transmission or pandemic-level spread of ANDV. Third - Expansion of reservoir host range may contribute to broader geographic dissemination and increased opportunities for human exposure. Orthohantaviruses were historically considered highly host-specific pathogens, with individual virus lineages predominantly associated with a single rodent reservoir species through long-term co-evolutionary relationships. ANDV is primarily associated with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir host. However, accumulating phylogenetic and ecological evidence has challenged the concept of strict host specificity, demonstrating that host-switching events, spillover infections, and reservoir diversification have likely occurred repeatedly throughout orthohantavirus evolutionary history. In addition, the identification of genetically divergent orthohantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats suggests that ancestral orthohantaviruses may have undergone multiple historical cross-species transmission events. Collectively, these findings indicate that orthohantavirus host associations, although generally stable, are not biologically absolute. Habitat disruptions, altered species interactions, and environmental pressures could therefore increase opportunities for cross-species transmission and geographic expansion over extended ecological timescales, potentially increasing the frequency of human exposure to infected reservoir hosts. Nevertheless, there is currently no evidence that such ecological processes have resulted in ANDV lineages with enhanced sustained human-to-human transmissibility. Current preparedness against ANDV outbreaks Perhaps more worrying is the limited availability of rapid diagnostics, antivirals, and vaccines for responding to outbreaks of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses. Several antiviral and immunotherapeutic strategies have been explored against human disease-causing orthohantaviruses, including nucleoside analogues such as ribavirin, favipiravir and ETAR; entry inhibitors such as lactoferrin and griffithsin; host-directed approaches targeting vascular leakage pathways; RNAi-based strategies; and, more recently, neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoprotein complex. However, no orthohantavirus-specific antiviral has yet become an established standard of care, and most candidates remain experimental or dependent on very early administration. In parallel, vaccine development efforts have advanced substantially over the past decades. Hantavax®, an inactivated orthohantavirus vaccine marketed in South Korea to prevent HFRS caused by Hantaan and Seoul viruses, remains among the only orthohantavirus vaccines licensed for human use, while several next-generation vaccine candidates are currently under development and evaluation in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Despite these advances, effective countermeasures specifically targeting ANDV remain limited, highlighting an important preparedness gap for future outbreaks. In conclusion - Overall, current evidence does not support the conclusion that ANDV is imminently poised to emerge as a pandemic pathogen comparable to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Nevertheless, under favourable ecological and epidemiological conditions, localised ANDV outbreaks may increase in scale or geographic distribution, potentially posing broader regional public health challenges. These considerations underscore the importance of strengthening preparedness strategies to prevent the escalation of orthohantavirus outbreaks, particularly in under-resourced endemic regions of South America. Integrated ecological surveillance approaches, including climate-informed forecasting of rodent population dynamics, together with genomic epidemiological surveillance of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses, may improve early detection of spillover risk, characterise orthohantavirus diversity and evolutionary dynamics, and support timely public health responses. In addition, expanded availability of antiviral therapeutics, monoclonal antibodies, preventive vaccines, and rapid diagnostic platforms will be important for comprehensive orthohantavirus outbreak preparedness and response. These diagnostic platforms could include lateral-flow assays to detect orthohantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies in symptomatic patients, as well as antigen-based tests for direct virus detection in both humans and reservoir hosts. analysis.background: The paper examines whether Andes virus (ANDV), a hantavirus capable of limited person‑to‑person transmission, could evolve into a pandemic threat, a concern highlighted by a recent cruise‑ship outbreak.
analysis.methods: An outbreak investigation was conducted after 13 ANDV cases were identified on the M/V Hondius (May–July 2026); public‑health actions included case isolation, quarantine, contact tracing, active surveillance, and genomic sequencing of viral S, M and L segments from cases.
analysis.results: Thirteen cases (3 deaths) were reported; viral genomes showed identical S and M segments and only two synonymous SNPs in the L segment, with ~98.7% nucleotide identity to historic Argentine strains, and incubation periods of 9–45 days, indicating limited transmission and no amino‑acid changes linked to increased spread.
analysis.contribution: The study underscores the low current pandemic risk of ANDV while highlighting ecological and evolutionary factors that could elevate future threat, thereby informing surveillance, diagnostic, therapeutic, and vaccine preparedness strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract and partial‑text information are provided; detailed epidemiological data, sample sizes, and comprehensive statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The paper examines whether Andes virus (ANDV), a hantavirus capable of limited person‑to‑person transmission, could evolve into a pandemic threat, a concern highlighted by a recent cruise‑ship outbreak. Methods: An outbreak investigation was conducted after 13 ANDV cases were identified on the M/V Hondius (May–July 2026); public‑health actions included case isolation, quarantine, contact tracing, active surveillance, and genomic sequencing of viral S, M and L segments from cases. Results: Thirteen cases (3 deaths) were reported; viral genomes showed identical S and M segments and only two synonymous SNPs in the L segment, with ~98.7% nucleotide identity to historic Argentine strains, and incubation periods of 9–45 days, indicating limited transmission and no amino‑acid changes linked to increased spread. Contribution: The study underscores the low current pandemic risk of ANDV while highlighting ecological and evolutionary factors that could elevate future threat, thereby informing surveillance, diagnostic, therapeutic, and vaccine preparedness strategies. Limitations: Only abstract and partial‑text information are provided; detailed epidemiological data, sample sizes, and comprehensive statistical analyses are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 能否让汉坦病毒驶向下一场大流行?

analysis_zh.background: 本文探讨安第斯病毒(ANDV)是否作为一种能够有限人际传播的汉坦病毒,可能演变为大流行威胁,此前一次近期的邮轮爆发凸显了该担忧。
analysis_zh.methods: 在M/V Hondius号(2026年5–7月)确认13例ANDV后开展了暴发调查;公共卫生措施包括病例隔离、检疫、接触者追踪、主动监测以及对病例病毒S、M、L片段的基因组测序。
analysis_zh.results: 报告13例(其中3例死亡);病毒基因组显示S、M片段完全相同,L片段仅有两个同义SNP,与历史阿根廷株的核苷酸相似度约为98.7%,潜伏期为9–45天,表明传播有限且未出现与传播增强相关的氨基酸变化。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究强调了当前ANDV的大流行风险仍然较低,同时指出可能提升未来威胁的生态和进化因素,为监测、诊断、治疗和疫苗预备策略提供参考。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要和部分正文信息;未报告详细的流行病学数据、样本量及完整的统计分析。

papers.title: Hantaviruses as Emerging Zoonotic Pathogens: Molecular Biology, Epidemiology, Therapeutics, vaccine, and Pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens belonging to the family Hantaviridae and are responsible for two major human diseases, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome.
analysis.main_directions: Key challenges include elucidating viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology.
analysis.current_state: The review adopts a One Health framework linking molecular virology, host‑virus interactions, transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and mechanisms of vascular leakage and severe disease.
analysis.gaps: Unresolved issues involve host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the lack of effective antivirals and vaccines.
analysis.future_research: Priorities are defined for enhanced surveillance, prevention strategies, and therapeutic development, integrating ecological and molecular insights.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS worldwide. Main directions: Major challenges lie in linking viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission, and host immunopathology. Current state: A One Health view connects molecular virology, host interactions, ecology, epidemiology, and disease mechanisms. Gaps: Host susceptibility, persistence, virulence determinants, interspecies spread, and therapeutic/vaccine gaps remain. Future research: Focus on integrated surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒es 作为新兴的动物源性病原体:分子生物学、流行病学、治疗学、疫苗及发病机制。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是全球分布的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 关键挑战包括阐明病毒进化、宿主储存生态、环境变化、传播动力学以及宿主免疫病理学。
analysis_zh.current_state: 本综述采用 One Health 框架,关联分子病毒学、宿主‐病毒相互作用、传播生态、全球流行病学以及血管渗漏和重症机制。
analysis_zh.gaps: 未解决的问题包括宿主易感性、病毒持久性、致病性和组织嗜性的决定因素、跨种传播,以及缺乏有效的抗病毒药物和疫苗。
analysis_zh.future_research: 已确定的重点是加强监测、预防策略和治疗研发,融合生态和分子洞察。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒es 是全球分布的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征。 主要方向：关键挑战包括阐明病毒进化、宿主储存生态、环境变化、传播动力学以及宿主免疫病理学。 研究现状：本综述采用 One Health 框架,关联分子病毒学、宿主‐病毒相互作用、传播生态、全球流行病学以及血管渗漏和重症机制。 不足：未解决的问题包括宿主易感性、病毒持久性、致病性和组织嗜性的决定因素、跨种传播,以及缺乏有效的抗病毒药物和疫苗。 后续研究：已确定的重点是加强监测、预防策略和治疗研发,融合生态和分子洞察。

papers.title: Expanded protocadherin-1 usage reveals a broader hantavirus entry landscape.
papers.abstract: Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses identified across Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas, we generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. Except for rVSV-Kenkeme, these rVSVs did not acquire additional mutations beyond pre-engineered rescue-enhancing changes during rescue and passaging. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova phenotype was weaker. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme rVSVs, but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam rVSVs. Together, these findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted strategies with differential activity.IMPORTANCEMany newly discovered hantaviruses are known only from sequence data, leaving their ability to enter human cells and their receptor usage unresolved. Using a BSL2-compatible recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) system, we show that glycoproteins from several divergent hantaviruses can mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. We also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors.

analysis.background: Mammalian hantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia, yet the cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined.
analysis.methods: Researchers generated replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from seven phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses and evaluated infection of primary human endothelial cells, including PCDH1‑knockout cells, to assess receptor usage.
analysis.results: All Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported entry into primary human endothelial cells; Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses required PCDH1 for efficient infection (Nova weaker); soluble PCDH1 and a PCDH1‑targeting monoclonal antibody blocked entry of Necoclí and Tula; authentic Tula infection was reduced in PCDH1‑KO endothelial cells; a broadly reactive anti‑Gn/Gc human monoclonal antibody neutralized several rVSVs but showed weak or no activity against others.
analysis.contribution: These findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1‑dependent entry, and identify receptor‑targeted and glycoprotein‑targeted inhibition strategies with differential activity.
analysis.limitations: The study relied on a surrogate rVSV system and in‑vitro cell models; no in‑vivo or clinical data were presented, and the breadth of viruses tested remains limited; not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Mammalian hantaviruses cause severe disease, but most entry mechanisms are unknown. Methods: rVSVs bearing Gn/Gc from seven diverse hantaviruses were used to infect primary human endothelial cells, including PCDH1‑knockout cells. Results: All except Kenkeme mediated entry; Necoclí, Tula, and Nova required PCDH1 (Nova weaker); soluble PCDH1 and a monoclonal antibody blocked Necoclí and Tula; authentic Tula infection was reduced in PCDH1‑KO cells; a broad anti‑Gn/Gc antibody neutralized several but not all viruses. Contribution: The work broadens the known hantavirus entry landscape, extends PCDH1 usage, and highlights receptor‑ and glycoprotein‑targeted inhibition strategies. Limitations: Relies on surrogate rVSV and in‑vitro assays; no in‑vivo data; limited virus panel; not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 扩展的protocadherin-1利用揭示了更广泛的 汉坦病毒 进入格局。

analysis_zh.background: 哺乳动物汉坦病毒在美洲导致汉坦病毒心肺综合征,在欧亚导致肾综合征出血热,但大多数汉坦病毒的细胞进入机制仍未明晰。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员构建了携带七种系统发育上不同的汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 蛋白的可复制重组水疱性口炎病毒(rVSV),并在原代人类内皮细胞(包括PCDH1基因敲除细胞)中评估感染,以检测受体使用情况。
analysis_zh.results: 除 Kenkeme 外,所有 Gn/Gc 蛋白均可介导原代人类内皮细胞的进入;Necoclí、Tula 和 Nova 病毒的高效感染依赖 PCDH1(Nova 较弱);可溶性 PCDH1 及针对 PCDH1 的单克隆抗体阻断了 Necoclí 和 Tula 的进入;在 PCDH1‐KO 内皮细胞中,真实的 Tula 感染被降低;一种广谱抗 Gn/Gc 人源单克隆抗体中和了多种 rVSV,但对其他病毒活性弱或无效。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现扩大了能够介导人类内皮细胞感染的 汉坦病毒 糖蛋白的范围,拓宽了 PCDH1 依赖性进入的系统发育范围,并确定了具有差异活性的受体靶向和糖蛋白靶向抑制策略。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本研究依赖于替代的 rVSV 系统和体外细胞模型;未提供体内或临床数据,且所测试病毒的范围仍受限;未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Vascular Programs in Emerging and Re-Emerging RNA Virus Infections: Comparative Lessons from SARS-CoV-2, Flaviviruses, and Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging RNA viruses frequently present with clinical phenotypes that extend beyond classical organ tropism and include vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation. SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial–coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet–leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

papers.title_zh: 新发与再发RNA病毒感染中的血管程序:来自SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒及汉坦病毒的比较经验

analysis_zh.background: 新发RNA病毒常引起血管渗漏、凝血失衡和血栓炎症,超出传统的器官嗜性。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述将SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒和汉坦病毒es作为病毒诱导血管疾病的模型,概述四个相互重叠的血管程序:内皮激活、屏障失效、凝血激活和血小板功能障碍。
analysis_zh.current_state: 这些程序解释了在不同病毒中观察到的血栓性、出血性和渗漏表型的范围,突显了共享的内皮‐凝血机制。

analysis_zh.future_research: 本文提出可检验的预测,包括跨病毒生物标志物面板、器官特异性内皮模型以及表型导向的临床研究。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：新发RNA病毒常引起血管渗漏、凝血失衡和血栓炎症,超出传统的器官嗜性。 主要方向：本综述将SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒和汉坦病毒es作为病毒诱导血管疾病的模型,概述四个相互重叠的血管程序:内皮激活、屏障失效、凝血激活和血小板… 研究现状：这些程序解释了在不同病毒中观察到的血栓性、出血性和渗漏表型的范围,突显了共享的内皮‐凝血机制。 不足：该框架为概念性而非定量分类,因而对具体的生物标志物阈值和因果通路仍存不确定性。 后续研究：本文提出可检验的预测,包括跨病毒生物标志物面板、器官特异性内皮模型以及表型导向的临床研究。

papers.title: IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS
papers.abstract: The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non-segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections.

World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 970 1 INTRODUCTION Viruses are ubiquitous in nature, infecting and proliferating in organisms across all kingdoms of life. They have evolved and adapted their lifecycles to the organisms they infect and, following successful infection, viruses rely predominantly on their host’s cellular machinery for their survival and proliferation. Based on the nature of their genome, viruses are broadly classified into RNA and DNA viruses. Both types cause diseases in plants, animals and humans, ranging from endemic to pandemic proportions, resulting in major global healthcare crises and unprecedented economic losses, necessitating a deeper understanding of their pathogenic and replication mechanisms to develop effective therapeutic interventions [1]. However, the majority of the serious human diseases are caused by RNA viruses belonging to both negative- and positive-strand viruses [2]. For example, Measles, Mumps, Human influenza viruses (A, B and C), Hendra, Cedar, Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Rabies, etc. are caused by the non-segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses whereas SARS-CoVs, MERS-CoV, Polio, Hepatitis C, Dengue, Zika, Yellow fever, Rubella, Encephalomyocarditis, HIVs, etc. belong to non-segmented, but positive-strand RNA viruses. Again, some of the RNA viruses possess segmented, single-stranded genomes like human influenza viruses (8 segments) and hantaviruses (3 segments), whereas some possess segmented, double-stranded RNA genomes like rotavirus and bluetongue virus. Hantaviruses are emerging human pathogens that cause severe, often fatal, hemorrhagic fevers and pulmonary syndromes. They have been responsible for several human disease outbreaks in recent years. Furthermore, human-to- human transmission in recent years has established hantaviruses as one of the most dangerous viruses [3, 4]. In fact, hantaviruses are more serious and lethal than the SARS-CoV-2, as some of them have a greater mortality rate (~50%) than the latter (~1% global average). Mostly hantaviruses are not transmitted between humans. However, the Andes orthohantavirus in South America has demonstrated limited person-to-person transmission, particularly among those in close contact. For example, recently, an outbreak of the Andes orthohantavirus on a cruise ship infected 11 people and killed three earlier this year (2026). Hantavirus was first discovered following the Korean War. During the war, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) was a common ailment in soldiers stationed near the Hantan River. This illness is now considered as one of the most serious haemorrhagic diseases in the world, like Ebola haemorrhagic fever, due to its high mortality rate and epidemic potential. The first hantavirus was isolated in 1978 in South Korea and was named Hantaan virus. Based on the geographic distribution, hantaviruses are broadly classified into Old World hantaviruses, which typically cause HFRS and are prevalent in Africa, Asia, and Europe, (e.g., Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc.) and New World hantaviruses (e.g., Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus, Choclo virus, etc.) which are associated with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas [5, 6]. The hantaviruses are primarily rodent-borne and are the main source of human infections, although new hantaviruses have recently been reported or isolated from bats, moles and shrews [7, 8]. Spillover of these viruses to humans can result in one of the two serious illnesses. The case fatality rate of HFRS ranges from 1% to 15%, while for HPS, it is 30–60% [9]. Thus, both diseases can be fatal, but with differing mortality rates. Currently, there is neither an approved vaccine nor a specific and effective antiviral treatment available for human use. Importantly, hantaviruses can survive for 10 days at room temperature, 15 days in temperate environments and more than 18 days at 4 °C (39 °F), which facilitates their stable transmission [9, 10]. Therefore, understanding the structure of the hantavirus genome and the functions of the key viral proteins is critical for developing effective antiviral therapeutic agents to control the spread of the virus. 1.1 Classification of hantaviruses Hantaviruses belong to the genus Orthohantavirus and the order Bunyavirales within the family of Hantaviridae. They are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses that cause two potentially lethal zoonotic syndromes, viz. HFRS and HPS as discussed elsewhere. It is estimated that, globally, around 1.5 million people get infected with hantaviruses each year with typical case fatality rates of up to 15 % for HFRS and around 40 % or higher for HPS [11]. Hantaviruses are further classified into Old World (HFRS-causing) and New World (HPS-causing) viruses [3]. The Old World hantaviruses are primarily found in Europe and Asia and typically cause HFRS with a mortality rate of up to 15%. Examples include, Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc. The New World hantaviruses are more dangerous and prevalent in North and South America and are associated with HPS with mortality rates reaching up to 40%. Examples include, Sin Nombre virus, Andes virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus. Choclo virus, etc. [12]. Among the hantaviruses, only the New World Andes virus has been demonstrated to have the potential for human-to-human transmission [4]. 1.2 3’→5’ PR exonucleases and their classifications PR exonucleases (EC 3.1.11.x) are ubiquitous enzymes that play a crucial role in repairing error(s) during replication of genomes and thus, maintain the integrity of genomes in organisms. They remove misincorporated wrong nucleotides in the 3′→ 5′ direction during DNA/RNA synthesis. Based on their conserved active site amino acids, these enzymes are broadly classified into two superfamilies, viz. the DEDD and the Polymerase and Histidinol Phosphatase (PHP) superfamilies [13, 14]. The DEDD superfamily is the most common type of PR enzyme and is reported from both DNA World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 971 and RNA polymerases from a large number of organisms from viruses to humans. The name derives from the four highly conserved acidic amino acid residues, viz. DEDD, in its active site for metal-binding and catalysis. The PHP superfamily, characterized by the active site amino acid structure, HxH-E-H-D, uses His residues for metal-binding and catalysis. Bacterial/Archaeal DNA polymerases X, bacterial DNA polymerases III (bacterial replicases) with a co-editing, built-in exonuclease [14, 15] and YcdX phosphoesterases [16] belong to PHP superfamily. Both superfamilies are essentially Zn- dependent enzymes and initiate the catalysis from a metal-bound water molecule [17]. It is interesting to note that certain viruses like the human influenza viruses use both types of PR exonucleases [18]. Furthermore, the DEDD superfamily is further classified into two subfamilies, viz. DEDD(Y) and DEDD(H), depending on whether they employ an invariant Y or a H as the proton acceptor during catalysis [Table 1]. Most of the RNA and DNA viruses possess a typical DEDD superfamily of 3′→5′ PR exoribonuclease in their genome and are well-characterized. For example, in SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV, it is characterized in the ExoN of the non-structural protein 14 along with the methyltransferase domain [17]. But in the other bat-borne viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah, a DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain was identified in the PRNTase (the capping enzyme) domain [19]. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease has also been reported in DNA viruses like smallpox, monkeypox viruses, etc. [Table 1] suggesting the same PR mechanism is used by both types of viruses. In contrast to their ubiquitous presence in RNA and DNA viruses, in hantaviruses it was reported that there was no demonstrated, dedicated proofreading exonuclease [20, 21]. However, in the present communication, a putative DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain, preceding the RdRp domain, has been identified featuring an invariant Y as the proton acceptor. 1.3 Importance of 3ʹ→5ʹ PR exonuclease as a potential drug target for controlling RNA viruses Maintenance of genome stability is essential for all living organisms and it mainly relies on the error-free replication of genomes by the respective DNA and RNA replicases. The genome stability is equally important for viruses also. This is because too many uncorrected mutations during replications could lead to an "error catastrophe," where the viruses could literally mutate itself to death. To overcome this problem, the RNA and DNA polymerases/replicases exhibit strong discrimination between nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) and deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) and rarely insert a wrong nucleotide during replication of genomes and hence, their error rates are very, very low and is usually in the order of ~10-4 to 10-6 and ~10-6-10-9, respectively [22]. To overcome even this minimal error rates during replications, these crucial polymerases of life are invariably associated with PR mechanisms that correct any insertion error(s) during replication. When an incorrect nucleotide gets incorporated during replication, the polymerases stall/pause, which in-turn activates the associated PR function, which promptly excises the misincorporated nucleotide. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases operates in the 3’→5’ direction and excise any incorrectly incorporated nucleotide from the 3’-growing end, and thus, helping the polymerases to perform error-free replication of genomes. Following the excision of the wrong nucleotide, the correct nucleotide is inserted and the polymerases resume the replication. This critical PR step in living organisms and viruses ensures that the original DNA/RNA template is copied accurately and passed on to the next generation. For example, with the PR 3'→ 5' exonuclease activity, the error rate dramatically improves to an accuracy of about 10−7 to 10−8 (one mistake per 10 million to 100 million bases). And further, with cellular mismatch repair, the final error rate drops as low as 10−9 to 10−11 per base pair (i.e., about one mistake per 1 billion bases) [23]. Thus, the PR functions play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of genomes in all organisms including the viruses. It is interesting to note that a SARS-CoV-2 PR exonuclease knockout mutant was unable to replicate, suggesting possibilities for development of effective antivirals directing the PR exonucleases to contain the spread of RNA viruses [17]. 1.4 Genome and L protein organizations in hantaviruses Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Orthomyxoviridae are the principal families of segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, and each of them include serious human pathogens. Arenaviridae have two genome segments, whereas Bunyaviridae and Orthomyxoviridae have three and six to eight genome segments, respectively. Arenaviruses and bunyaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm using a single subunit RdRp of the L protein, whereas the orthomyxoviruses replicate in the nucleus- an unusual trait of an RNA virus- using a heterotrimeric polymerase complex composed of PA, PB1 and PB2 subunits [18]. Hantaviruses are segmented, negative-strand, enveloped viruses which belong to the order Bunyavirales, Family, Hantaviridae, and Genus, Orthohantavirus. Unlike other human pathogenic viruses, they are primarily carried by rodents. The virions are generally spherical to pleomorphic, measuring approximately 80-160 nm in diameter, although the size may vary among species. Thus, the segmented, tripartite RNA genome of hantaviruses consists of a small (S), a medium (M), and a large (L) segment and encodes only four structural proteins. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA genome segments to form ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes and plays key roles in viral replication and immune modulation. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor that is post-translationally cleaved into two envelope glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are essential for viral attachment and entry into host cells. The multidomain L segment encodes a viral RdRp, responsible for both transcription and replication and a cap- snatching endonuclease, responsible for snatching mRNA caps from the host mRNAs for priming the viral mRNAs. The World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 972 genomic RNA segments are encapsidated by the nucleocapsid protein P, to form helical RNP complexes, which are enclosed within a host-derived lipid envelope studded with Gn and Gc glycoprotein spikes. [24]. The viral envelope is derived from host cell membranes and contains the above embedded glycoprotein spikes that facilitate interaction with host cell receptors. The tripartite genome segments form into circles via non-covalent interactions of the ends of the genome with an attached L protein to initiate transcription upon entry into host cells. The 3'- and 5'- terminal nucleotides are highly conserved and complementary in all three genome segments that form a conserved panhandle structure acting as the viral promoter in each of the genome segment. In addition to the coding region, each segment possesses short untranslated regions (UTRs) at the 5′ and 3′ termini. The 3' and 5' UTRs are highly conserved and regulate replication and transcription of the genomes [25].
