They are embedded in the lipid bilayer and form characteristic spikes. They are involved in host cell attachment and entry. • The large segment encodes the L protein, an approximately 250 kDa protein harbouring the RdRp. The L protein is a multifunctional protein that harbours an N-terminal endonuclease (EndoN), an RdRp, and a presumed cap binding domain (CBD) at the C-terminal (CTD) and organised as: Endonuclease 1-372; PR Exo 373-676; RdRp 677-1601; CTD 1602-2151. • Importantly, each of the genome segments carries the L protein polymerase to initiate the transcription upon entry and unc…

full_text_sections.full_text: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 969 IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS Peramachi Palanivelu * Department of Molecular Microbiology, School of Biotechnology, Madurai Kamaraj University, Madurai – 625 021, India. * Corresponding Author World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 Publication history: Received on 06 September 2026; revised on 12 October 2026; accepted on 14 October 2026 Article DOI: https://doi.org/10.30574/wjarr.2026.32.1.2621 Copyright © 2026 Author(s) retain the copyright of this article. This article is published under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License 4.0 ABSTRACT The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non- segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections. Keywords: Hantaviruses, Old World hantaviruses, New World hantaviruses, 3’→5’ proofreading exonucleases, DEDD superfamily of proofreading exonucleases. World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 970 1 INTRODUCTION Viruses are ubiquitous in nature, infecting and proliferating in organisms across all kingdoms of life. They have evolved and adapted their lifecycles to the organisms they infect and, following successful infection, viruses rely predominantly on their host’s cellular machinery for their survival and proliferation. Based on the nature of their genome, viruses are broadly classified into RNA and DNA viruses. Both types cause diseases in plants, animals and humans, ranging from endemic to pandemic proportions, resulting in major global healthcare crises and unprecedented economic losses, necessitating a deeper understanding of their pathogenic and replication mechanisms to develop effective therapeutic interventions [1]. However, the majority of the serious human diseases are caused by RNA viruses belonging to both negative- and positive-strand viruses [2]. For example, Measles, Mumps, Human influenza viruses (A, B and C), Hendra, Cedar, Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Rabies, etc. are caused by the non-segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses whereas SARS-CoVs, MERS-CoV, Polio, Hepatitis C, Dengue, Zika, Yellow fever, Rubella, Encephalomyocarditis, HIVs, etc. belong to non-segmented, but positive-strand RNA viruses. Again, some of the RNA viruses possess segmented, single-stranded genomes like human influenza viruses (8 segments) and hantaviruses (3 segments), whereas some possess segmented, double-stranded RNA genomes like rotavirus and bluetongue virus. Hantaviruses are emerging human pathogens that cause severe, often fatal, hemorrhagic fevers and pulmonary syndromes. They have been responsible for several human disease outbreaks in recent years. Furthermore, human-to- human transmission in recent years has established hantaviruses as one of the most dangerous viruses [3, 4]. In fact, hantaviruses are more serious and lethal than the SARS-CoV-2, as some of them have a greater mortality rate (~50%) than the latter (~1% global average). Mostly hantaviruses are not transmitted between humans. However, the Andes orthohantavirus in South America has demonstrated limited person-to-person transmission, particularly among those in close contact. For example, recently, an outbreak of the Andes orthohantavirus on a cruise ship infected 11 people and killed three earlier this year (2026). Hantavirus was first discovered following the Korean War. During the war, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) was a common ailment in soldiers stationed near the Hantan River. This illness is now considered as one of the most serious haemorrhagic diseases in the world, like Ebola haemorrhagic fever, due to its high mortality rate and epidemic potential. The first hantavirus was isolated in 1978 in South Korea and was named Hantaan virus. Based on the geographic distribution, hantaviruses are broadly classified into Old World hantaviruses, which typically cause HFRS and are prevalent in Africa, Asia, and Europe, (e.g., Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc.) and New World hantaviruses (e.g., Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus, Choclo virus, etc.) which are associated with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas [5, 6]. The hantaviruses are primarily rodent-borne and are the main source of human infections, although new hantaviruses have recently been reported or isolated from bats, moles and shrews [7, 8]. Spillover of these viruses to humans can result in one of the two serious illnesses. The case fatality rate of HFRS ranges from 1% to 15%, while for HPS, it is 30–60% [9]. Thus, both diseases can be fatal, but with differing mortality rates. Currently, there is neither an approved vaccine nor a specific and effective antiviral treatment available for human use. Importantly, hantaviruses can survive for 10 days at room temperature, 15 days in temperate environments and more than 18 days at 4 °C (39 °F), which facilitates their stable transmission [9, 10]. Therefore, understanding the structure of the hantavirus genome and the functions of the key viral proteins is critical for developing effective antiviral therapeutic agents to control the spread of the virus. 1.1 Classification of hantaviruses Hantaviruses belong to the genus Orthohantavirus and the order Bunyavirales within the family of Hantaviridae. They are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses that cause two potentially lethal zoonotic syndromes, viz. HFRS and HPS as discussed elsewhere. papers.title: Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 10 1 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

papers.title: Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis
papers.abstract: The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets.

Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets.

Aiyelabola, Sayantan Pradhan, and Takashiro Akitsu, “Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis.” Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, vol. 14, no. 1 (2026): 1-14. doi: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1. 1. Introduction Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents [1,2]. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide [3]. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) [4,5,6]. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor 2 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry progression and poor clinical prognosis [7]. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis [10]. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer [11]. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) [8,9,10,11]. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates [12]. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) [13]. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation [14]. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene- derived Schiff base ligand (N1). The primary objective of this study was to investigate its interaction with multiple breast cancer-associated kinase targets, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which collectively regulate tumor proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. As an exploratory extension of this computational investigation, the ligand was also docked against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein to assess whether this chemical scaffold exhibits potential binding capability toward a structurally unrelated viral protein involved in RNA encapsidation. This exploratory comparison should not be interpreted as evidence of a unified therapeutic strategy but rather as an initial computational assessment of the molecular recognition properties of N1 across biologically distinct protein targets. The ligand (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5- nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine, and its in silico activities are reported here for the first time. Figure 1. The figure illustrates the proposed mechanism of action of the investigated ligand against major breast cancer-associated signaling proteins, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K. Activation of EGFR and HER2 normally initiates downstream signaling cascades such as the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which promote cancer cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis. VEGFR2 activation stimulates angiogenic signaling pathways responsible for tumor vascularization and endothelial cell migration. In the proposed mechanism, inhibition of these receptors suppresses phosphorylation-mediated signaling events, thereby reducing tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastatic progression. PI3K inhibition further decreases AKT/mTOR signaling, leading to apoptosis induction and suppression of cancer cell survival. Overall, the figure demonstrates the multi-target inhibitory action of the ligand against critical pathways involved in breast cancer progression Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry 3 Figure 2. The figure represents the life cycle of Andes hantavirus and the proposed antiviral mechanism of the investigated compound targeting the viral nucleoprotein (N protein). The hantavirus initially enters the host cell through receptor-mediated endocytosis, followed by viral uncoating and release of ribonucleoprotein complexes into the cytoplasm. Viral RNA transcription and replication are subsequently carried out by the viral RNA- dependent RNA polymerase, leading to synthesis of viral proteins and assembly of new virions. The proposed ligand is suggested to bind within the RNA-binding region of the hantavirus nucleoprotein, thereby interfering with viral RNA encapsidation and ribonucleoprotein complex formation. This inhibition may suppress viral replication, reduce formation of mature viral particles, and prevent further viral dissemination within host cells. The overall antiviral outcome includes inhibition of viral replication, reduction of viral load, and prevention of hantavirus propagation 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Synthesis: Material All starting materials and solvents used were purchased from Aldrich and Fluka and were used without further purification. Melting points were determined in an open capillary tube on a Gallenkamp (Variable heater) melting point apparatus. NMR spectrum (1H) was recorded on an analysis X-685 benchtop NMR spectrophotometer at 60 MHz DMSO-d6 with TMS as internal standard, at the central science laboratory, Covenant University, Ota. The infrared spectra of all synthesized products were obtained using Agilent Cary 630 FTIR. The electronic spectra, of all the compounds, were obtained in solution, in the wavelength range 400-1000 nm using 1800 Shimadzu ultra-violet spectrophotometer. Both were carried out at the central science laboratory, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife. 2.2. Synthesis; Experimental An ethanolic solution of 1,8-diaminonaphthalene (0.83 g, 5.00 mmol) was introduced to a solution of 5-nitro-2- carboxaldehyde (1.62 g, 10.0 mmol) in absolute ethanol (25 mL) supplemented with glacial acetic acid (3 drops) as a catalyst. The reaction mixture was subjected to reflux conditions for 4 hours under atmospheric pressure. Following thermal treatment, the reaction vessel was allowed to equilibrate to ambient temperature, after which the volatile organic solvent was removed via rotary evaporation under reduced pressure until precipitation of a solid product occurred. The crude material was subsequently triturated with cold ethanol and subjected to recrystallization from a chloroform/ethanol solvent mixture (volume ratio 30:70). A deep orange-colored solid was obtained, collected by vacuum filtration, and dried under reduced pressure at 60°C until constant mass was achieved, yielding N1 as the isolated product. The compound demonstrated appreciable solubility in chloroform, ethanol, and methanol. The schematic representation for the preparation of N1 is given in Scheme 1. Yield: 1.49 g, 68.78%; m.p: 165 ̊C - 166 ̊C (d); IR (cm−1): 1608 ν(C=C), 1587 ν(C=N), 1423 ν(C=C, thiophene aromatic ring) 1490 and 1326 ν(NO2), UV-Vis (nm): 299; 1 H NMR (60 MHz): DMSO-d6 δ 7.95 (s, 1H), 7.21, 7.04 (d, 6H), 6.64, 6.55 (d, 2H). Scheme 1. Schematic representation of the synthesis pathway of the novel Schiff base ligand N1, (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2- yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine formed through the condensation reaction between 5-nitrothiophene-2-carbaldehyde and naphthalene-1,8- diamine. The figure also illustrates the optimized three-dimensional molecular structure of the synthesized compound 2.3. Retrieval of Protein Structures The three-dimensional crystal structures of the selected 4 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry therapeutic targets associated with breast cancer and viral infection were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The protein structures used in this study included epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, PDB ID: 1M17, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2, PDB ID: 3PP0), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2, PDB ID: 1YWN), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K, PDB ID: 4JPS), and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein (PDB ID: 5E04 ). The biologically relevant protein chain (Chain A) was selected for all docking studies. These structures were chosen based on their high crystallographic resolution and the presence of co- crystallized ligands within the active site, allowing accurate definition of the ligand-binding pocket for molecular docking. 2.4. Protein Preparation Protein preparation was performed using AutoDock Tools. Prior to docking, all crystallographic water molecules, co-crystallized ligands, and non-essential heteroatoms were removed while preserving the protein backbone and active-site residues. Polar hydrogen atoms were subsequently added, and Kollman united-atom partial charges were assigned to the protein structures. The prepared receptors were saved in PDBQT format for docking calculations [19]. 2.5. Ligand Preparation The chemical structure of the synthesized ligand was generated using ChemDraw Professional 12.0 and converted into a three-dimensional structure using Avogadro . Geometry optimization was carried out using the MMFF94 force field until convergence to obtain a minimum-energy conformation. Hydrogen atoms were added, appropriate protonation corresponding to physiological pH (approximately 7.4) was assigned, and Gasteiger partial atomic charges were calculated using AutoDock Tools. The optimized ligand was finally converted into PDBQT format for molecular docking [20,21]. 2.6. Molecular Docking Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina (version 1.2.7) to evaluate the binding affinity and binding mode of the ligand against the selected protein targets. The docking grid was centered on the active-site region defined by the co-crystallized ligand in each receptor structure. A grid box of 25 × 25 × 25 Å with a grid spacing of 1.0 Å was employed to adequately encompass the entire binding pocket. Docking calculations were carried out using an exhaustiveness value of 8, and 10 binding poses were generated for each protein-ligand complex. The resulting docking conformations were ranked according to their predicted binding free energies (kcal/mol). The optimal binding pose for each complex was selected based on the lowest binding free energy together with a favorable binding orientation and the formation of key interactions with biologically relevant active-site residues identified from the corresponding crystal structures and supported by previous literature [22,23]. 2.7. Drug-Likeness Evaluation The drug-likeness properties of N1 were evaluated using widely accepted computational pharmacokinetic filters, including Lipinski’s Rule of Five and Ghose’s filter, to assess its suitability as a potential orally active therapeutic agent. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, hydrogen bond acceptors, hydrogen bond donors, partition coefficient (logP), molar refractivity, and total number of atoms were calculated to determine the drug-like behavior and oral bioavailability of the compound [24,25]. Lipinski’s Rule of Five was applied based on the criteria of molecular weight below 500 Da, hydrogen bond acceptors fewer than 10, hydrogen bond donors fewer than 5, and logP value below 5, which are considered favorable for oral drug candidates [24]. In addition, Ghose’s filter was employed to further evaluate the compound by considering acceptable ranges of molecular weight, lipophilicity, molar refractivity, and atom count commonly associated with biologically active molecules [25]. All calculations and predictions were performed using an online ADMET and drug-likeness prediction platform. The obtained parameters were analyzed to determine the compliance of N1 with established drug- likeness criteria 2.8. papers.title: From Systemic Inflammation to Calcium Leak: The RyR2 Hypothesis of Reversible Myocardial Dysfunction in Andes Virus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. In severe disease, elevated IL-6, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and nitrosative stress activate pathways that in experimental models converge on RyR2 through CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation at Ser2814, oxidative modification of cysteine residues, and S-nitrosylation, each destabilizing the channel and promoting diastolic Ca2+ leak. The resulting increase in spontaneous Ca2+ release reduces SR Ca2+ content, impairs contractility, and predisposes to arrhythmias. This framework identifies RyR2 as a plausible mechanistic hub for the reversible cardiac phenotype. Therapeutic implications are discussed, emphasizing the timing of interventions and the potential of rycals, drugs that stabilize the closed state of RyR2 and prevent diastolic Ca2+ leak, as an emerging strategy. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.

analysis.background: HCPS caused by Andes virus shows profound but often reversible myocardial dysfunction without major structural damage (A1) and the pathways linking systemic inflammation to this phenotype remain unclear (A2).
analysis.main_directions: The review proposes that inflammatory mediators converge on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2) via post‑translational modifications (A3), describing IL‑6, ROS/RNS–driven CaMKII phosphorylation, oxidation and S‑nitrosylation that destabilize RyR2 (A4), and discusses RyR2‑stabilizing agents (rycals) as a therapeutic concept (A7).
analysis.current_state: Experimental data show that these modifications cause diastolic Ca²⁺ leak, reduced SR Ca²⁺ load, impaired contractility and arrhythmia risk (A5), supporting RyR2 as a plausible hub for reversible dysfunction (A6).
analysis.gaps: The precise causal chain from inflammation to RyR2 dysfunction in humans is unproven (A2) and the hypothesis lacks in‑vivo validation and clinical trials (A8).
analysis.future_research: Studies should test RyR2‑targeted interventions such as rycals in animal models and HCPS patients, and delineate the temporal relationship of cytokine spikes, RyR2 modifications, and cardiac outcomes (A7, A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by Andes virus shows profound but often reversible myocardial dysfunction without major structural damage (A1) and the pathways linking systemic inflammation to this phenotype remain unclear (A2). Main directions: The review proposes that inflammatory mediators converge on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2) via post‑translational modifications (A3), describing IL‑6, ROS/RNS–driven CaMKII phosphorylation, oxidation and S‑nitrosylation that destabilize RyR2 (A4), and discusses RyR2‑stabilizing agents (rycals) as a therapeutic concept (A7). Current state: Experimental data show that these modifications cause diastolic Ca²⁺ leak, reduced SR Ca²⁺ load, impaired contractility and arrhythmia risk (A5), supporting RyR2 as a plausible hub for reversible dysfunction (A6). Gaps: The precise causal chain from inflammation to RyR2 dysfunction in humans is unproven (A2) and the hypothesis lacks in‑vivo validation and clinical trials (A8). Future research: Studies should test RyR2‑targeted interventions such as rycals in animal models and HCPS patients, and delineate the temporal relationship of cytokine spikes, RyR2 modifications, and cardiac outcomes (A7, A8).

papers.title_zh: 从全身性炎症到钙泄漏:安第斯病毒心肺综合征中可逆性心肌功能障碍的RyR2假说

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 引起的汉坦病毒心肺综合征表现出显著但常可逆的心肌功能障碍,且无明显结构性损伤 (A1),系统性炎症与该表型之间的关联通路尚不清楚 (A2)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 综述提出炎症介质通过翻译后修饰作用于心脏雷诺受体 (RyR2) (A3),阐述 IL‐6、ROS/RNS 介导的 CaMKII 磷酸化、氧化及 S‐亚硝基化导致 RyR2 不稳定 (A4),并讨论以 RyR2 稳定剂 (rycals) 为治疗概念 (A7)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 实验数据表明这些修饰导致舒张期 Ca2+ 泄漏、SR Ca2+ 储备下降、收缩功能受损及心律失常风险增加 (A5),支持 RyR2 作为可逆功能障碍的潜在枢纽 (A6)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 炎症至人类 RyR2 功能障碍的精确因果链尚未得到证实 (A2),且该假设缺乏体内验证和临床试验 (A8)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 研究应在动物模型和汉坦病毒心肺综合征患者中测试以 RyR2 为靶点的干预措施,如 rycals,并阐明细胞因子峰值、RyR2 修饰与心脏结局之间的时间关系 (A7, A8)。

papers.title: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad compound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats.
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral ther- apeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats. KEYWORDS antiviral discovery, drug development, orthohantavirus, chemotherapeutics, phytochemicals, viral entry inhibitors, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitors, viral life cycle targets Introduction The April 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship served as a reminder of the ongoing challenges pathogens pose to global public health (Andes Virus Outbreak Working Group, 2026; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026; World Health Organization, 2026b). The high case fatality rate highlights that there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines against orthohantavirus infections (World Health Organization, 2026a). These rodent-borne pathogens belong to the family Hantaviridae, genus Orthohantavirus, and are enveloped, tri-segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA viruses (Jonsson et al., 2010). They cause two distinct, life-threatening clinical syndromes, one being Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia, and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (Heyman et al., 2009). The latter carries a severe case fatality rate reaching up to 54.3% (Campos et al., 2009), Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 01 OPEN ACCESS EDITED BY Henry Puerta-Guardo, Universidad Auto ́ noma de Yucata ́ n, Mexico REVIEWED BY Luis Adrian De Jesu ́ s-Gonza ́ lez, Mexican Social Security Institute, Mexico *CORRESPONDENCE Edison Luiz Durigon eldurigo@usp.br Carsten Wrenger cwrenger@icb.usp.br RECEIVED 19 August 2026 REVISED 14 September 2026 ACCEPTED 23 September 2026 PUBLISHED 16 October 2026 CITATION Kocabiyik DZ, de Araujo J, Durigon EL and Wrenger C (2026) Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions. Infection begins when the viral Gn protein docks onto host surface receptors, using integrin and protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Jangra et al., 2018). Once internalized via endocytosis, a drop in endosomal pH forces the viral envelope to fuse with the host membrane, releasing the genome into the cytoplasm. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) starts both transcription and genome replication, before structural proteins and newly synthesized RNA assemble at the Golgi complex or plasma membrane prior to budding out as mature infectious virions (see Figure 1) (Hussein et al., 2011; Hepojoki et al., 2012; Vaheri et al., 2013b; Bradfute et al., 2024). Current orthohantavirus management relies on supportive care and repurposed drugs with limited efficacy. To overcome this public health issue, this review presents existing treatment strategies and advocates for modern in silico approaches like molecular docking. Specifically, we highlight the potential of rational drug design, encouraging the systematic virtual screening of diverse chemical and natural product libraries to discover accessible, broad-spectrum hantaviral treatments. Viral entry and fusion inhibitors One of the most promising strategies to inhibit hantaviral entry into host cells is the use of cyclic peptides. With the help of a phage library, where peptide libraries are displayed on the surfaces of filamentous bacteriophages, Larson et al. (2005) identified cyclic nonapeptides that bind the b3-integrin receptor, which pathogenic orthohantaviruses like Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) bind for viral entry into human endothelial cells. Eleven of the 70 sequences showed inhibitory effects of >80% against SNV in vitro, the most potent of these, CPFVKTQLC, demonstrated high inhibitory FIGURE 1 The orthohantavirus life cycle and points of therapeutic intervention. Key stages of cellular infections are shown. Red crosses (X) indicate specific steps targeted by the therapeutic interventions discussed in the review. Adapted from Jonsson et al. (2010); Mir (2010); Vaheri et al. (2013b). cRNA, complementary RNA; L, Large segment; M, Medium segment; mRNA, messenger RNA; PCDH1, Protocadherin-1; RdRp, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; RNP, Ribonucleoprotein; S, Small segment; vRNA, viral RNA. Created with BioRender.com. Kocabiyik et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1972830 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 02 potency when presented by phage (IC50 = 2.7 x 108 particles/μL) (Larson et al., 2005). This peptide was further refined to its minimal functional unit required through alanine substitution and deletion scanning to the cyclic pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC] (Hall et al., 2007). However, because free monovalent peptides were less effec- tive than those presented on phage, subsequent research (Hall et al., 2008) shifted towards presenting peptides in a multivalent format on nanoparticles and targeting the orthohantavirus glycoproteins directly rather than the host b3-integrin receptor. The three most potent binders of the virion were selected and attached to 100 nm nanoparticles to create a multivalent inhibitor. When the peptide CLVRNLAWC was presented on a nanoparticle at a 4:1 ratio, its inhibition of SNV jumped from 9% (as a free peptide) to 32.5%. However, the peptide CQATTARNC achieved an even higher efficacy, with inhibition surpassing 50% when the nanoparticle- to-virus ratio was increased to 20:1 (Hall et al., 2008). Building on these strategies, the research was expanded to Andes virus (ANDV). Using a similar approach, Hall et al. (2009) eluted the peptide library from purified ANDV particles using monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the Gn and Gc glycoproteins. A major finding in this study was the combined use of peptides that targeted different Gn- and Gc-specific sequences resulted in synergistic inhibition (anti-Gc/Gn peptides CMQSAAAHC and CTVGPTRSC) of infec- tion that was significantly more powerful than single-peptide treatments, emphasizing the benefit of targeting multiple viral epitopes (Hall et al., 2009). Lastly, to search for peptidomimetic molecules to block SNV infection, Hall et al. (2010) used the 3D structure of the previously refined pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC], in a ligand-based virtual screening approach to evaluate over 600,000 small molecules. This transition from biological peptides to drug- like peptidomimetics identified compounds such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which were 2,000 times more potent than the original cyclic peptides. These molecules demonstrated high-affinity inhibi- tion in the nanomolar range in vitro (EC50 values between 1.3 - 2.5 nM) (Hall et al., 2010), successfully evolving the initial lead into a highly potent preclinical candidate warranting further in vivo evaluation. Another distinct strategy to prevent infection focuses on dis- rupting the viral membrane fusion process. Because the orthohantavirus Gc glycoprotein functions as a class II fusion protein, completing membrane fusion requires a major structural relocation of Domain III (DIII) to achieve the post-fusion state (Barriga et al., 2016; Arata-Salas et al., 2026). Exploiting this mechanical vulnerability, Barriga et al. (2016) demonstrated that viral entry can be successfully blocked using recombinant fragments and synthetic peptides derived from the Gc DIII and stem region. These fragments allow initial Gc trimerization to proceed but ultimately inhibit the pathway by preventing membrane hemifusion and fusion pore formation (Barriga et al., 2016). The recombinant DIII fragment inhibited ANDV fusion by around 70% at 25 μM and demonstrated cross-reactivity by reducing PUUV-mediated fusion by 50%. Even greater potency was observed with the R2 peptide, derived from the C-terminal part of the Gc stem region, which inhibited ANDV fusion by up to 95% in vitro (Barriga et al., 2016). Although efficacy dropped to a 70% cross-reduction (at 20 μM) against PUUV-mediated fusion (Barriga et al., 2016) due to its high genetic divergence between the two viruses, it still demonstrates significant cross-protective potential. Another very potent cell-entry inhibitor is Griffithsin (GRFT), an algae-derived lectin that has demonstrated high efficacy against several enveloped viruses such as coronaviruses, retroviruses, lentiviruses, flaviviruses, hepaciviruses, paramyxoviruses, and her- pesviruses, with the notable exclusion of gamma- and delta-retro- viruses. Interestingly, GRFT is also effective against the non- enveloped human papillomavirus (HPV), where it acts during a late step in the viral entry process rather than during initial attachment (O’Keefe et al., 2010; Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016). In vivo administration of GRFT demonstrated clear therapeutic effi- cacy, significantly mitigating disease severity and reducing mortality in lethal SARS-CoV infection models (O’Keefe et al., 2010). Highlighting its strong translational potential, GRFT has also advanced to phase I clinical trials against human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infections (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT04032717, NCT02875119). In addition to potent inhibition of ANDV entry (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), found that a synthetic trimeric variant (3mGRFT) possessing nine oligosaccha- ride-binding sites demonstrated even greater in vitro potency against ANDV and SNV. However, in contrast to its post-infection efficacy seen in other viral models (Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016), the authors observed that GRFT lacked potent inhibitory activity against ANDV post-infection. While GRFT showed in vitro effec- tivity against New World hantaviruses (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), the lectin inhibited HTNV in vivo and provided partial protection in suckling mice infected with HTNV (Zhao et al., 2022). Moreover, GRFT can be produced on a large scale and can be easily purified, highlighting its potential as an antiviral candidate for further preclinical testing against orthohantaviruses (Zhao et al., 2022). Exploring natural host defense proteins, bovine lactoferrin (LF) has demonstrated significant efficacy as a viral inhibitor against SEOV. LF prevents initial viral adsorption and adhesion, likely by interacting with cellular glycosaminoglycans such as heparin, or by sterically hindering the virus from binding to host b-integrin and lectin receptors (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Importantly, LF has no antiviral effect once the virus entered the host cell. In vivo, prophylactic administration of LF one day prior to orthohantavirus inoculation improved survival rates in mice up to 70% (at 160 mg/ kg), with a double-administration regimen enhancing survival to over 94%. Furthermore, when prophylactic LF treatment was combined with subsequent ribavirin administration, the two agents functioned synergistically, profoundly reducing viral shed- ding and completely inhibiting viral protein expression (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Discovered through a high-throughput screening of over 2,300 approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicines, cepharanthine (CEP), which is a compound isolated from Stephania cephalantha Hayata, has emerged as a highly potent viral entry and membrane fusion inhibitor. In vitro, CEP inhibited HTNV pseudovirus (EC50 value of 0.9 μM) and reduced viral nucleic acid copies by 73% at 20 μM. In vivo, administering CEP to Balb/c mice five hours post- infection significantly reduced infection by 93% (at 90 mg/kg/day) and 94% (at 180 mg/kg/day). Given its established safety profile, Kocabiyik et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1972830 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 03 CEP represents a high-priority candidate for repurposing and advancement into human clinical trials against orthohantaviruses (Wen et al., 2022). Viral replication and polymerase inhibitors Ribavirin (1-b- D-ribofuranosyl-1H-1,2,4-triazole-3- carboxamide; RBV), a synthetic guanosine nucleoside analogue, serves as the historical benchmark for anti-hantaviral therapy (Sidwell et al., 1972). Once it is transported into host cells, RBV is rapidly phosphorylated into metabolites such as RBV-5’-mono- phosphate (RBV-MP) and RBV-5’-triphosphate (RBV-TP). While RBV-MP inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), resulting in a decrease in intracellular GTP levels, RBV-TP selectively interacts with the viral RdRp as its primary mechanism of action (Severson et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2007). The incorporation of RBV leads to accumulation of genomic errors, and thus to dramatic loss of virus viability (“error catastrophe”) (Severson et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2007). Preclinical evaluation confirmed that early RBV administration reduces viral loads and prevents severe disease in suckling mouse models infected with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and hamster models infected with Andes virus (ANDV) (Huggins et al., 1986; Ogg et al., 2013). Clinically, intravenous RBV demonstrated efficacy in a double-blind, placebo- controlled trial of 242 patients with HTNV-induced HFRS, signif- icantly reducing hemorrhagic and overall mortality (Huggins et al., 1991). However, efficacy varies significantly across strains and clinical syndromes. In the context of HCPS caused by Andes virus (ANDV), intervention with RBV eliminated mortality com- pared to a 35% historical case-fatality rate and reduced the inci- dence of the severe cardiopulmonary phase from 84% to 57% (Strella et al., 2025). Conversely, in a larger placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial evaluating intravenous RBV for HCPS, the drug failed to demonstrate overall therapeutic efficacy, revealing no significant difference in survival (70% with RBV vs. 62% with placebo), nor in necessity of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) between groups (Mertz et al., 2004). Trials in HFRS caused by Puumala virus (PUUV) also showed insufficient efficacy and safety of intravenous RBV, likely due to delayed drug administra- tion and weaker correlation between viral load and disease severity compared to HTNV infection (Malinin and Platonov, 2017). Despite its status as an established treatment for HFRS, the clinical utility of RBV is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, most notably reversible hemolytic anemia, reported in 71% of recipients (Chapman et al., 1999; Jonsson et al., 2010). Furthermore, the lack of efficacy in HCPS and PUUV-caused HFRS is attributed to the rapid clinical progression of these diseases, which often leaves a narrow window for intervention before the onset of irreversible organ failure (Heyman et al., 2009; Vaheri et al., 2013a; Strella et al., 2025). Originally discovered by Toyama Chemical Co., Ltd., during a screening for anti-influenza compounds, the prodrug favipiravir (T- 705) has emerged as a potent viral replication inhibitor. Upon cellular entry, host enzymes convert favipiravir into its active form, favipiravir-RTP. This active metabolite functions as a purine nucleotide analogue that is incorporated into nascent viral RNA, inducing lethal mutagenesis in the viral genome (Furuta et al., 2009, 2017). Safronetz et al. (2013) have shown that favipiravir potently inhibited ANDV and SNV in vitro, and provided 100% survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia, making it an important drug candidate for post-exposure prophylaxis. To further enhance clinical outcomes, Mayor et al. (2021) combined the use of favipiravir with ribavirin to achieve synergistic orthohantavirus inhibition. papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 通过 One Health 视角的出现:生态动态、人类暴露与综合监测

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热和美洲的 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,其风险受宿主生态、环境变异和人类暴露的影响。
analysis_zh.methods: 本小型综述综合了来自中国、欧洲和美洲的证据,将啮齿动物、环境和人类数据关联,以评估 汉坦病毒 的出现。
analysis_zh.results: 汉坦病毒 的发病率取决于啮齿动物种群动态、气候条件、土地利用、农业实践、居住环境以及休闲或旅行相关的暴露;在中国呈现季节性高峰,而林纹田鼠循环则影响欧洲的 普马拉病毒 疫情。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本综述主张基于证据的 One Health 监测,将啮齿动物、环境和人类数据相结合,在流行季节发布风险预警,并在流行农业地区的收获期前加强减暴露措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

papers.full_text: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks Nyall Jamieson1,*, Rémy Pasco2, Sam Abbott3, Justin Lessler4,5,6, Lauren Ancel Meyers1,7 1Department of Integrative Biology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, United States of America 2BioFrontiers Institute, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, United States of America 3Centre for Mathematical modeling of Infectious Diseases, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, United Kingdom 4Department of Epidemiology, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States of America 5 UNC Carolina Population Center, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States of America 6Department of Epidemiology, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America 7Department of Statistics and Data Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, United States of America *Corresponding author: Nyall Jamieson. nyall.jamieson@austin.utexas.edu Abstract The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs. 1 Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 biological dependencies among infection, symptom onset, and infectiousness. Here, we extend the latent-time framework by integrating a mechanistic model that jointly links infection, symptom onset, and transmission [15]. We incorporate the resulting estimates in stochastic branching-process simulations of a multinational exposure event based on the initial timing and magnitude of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak. Given the variation in transmission observed across past ANDV events, we simulate outbreaks in both high- and low-transmission settings. The high-transmission setting uses parameters estimated from the Epuyén investigation, whereas the low-transmission setting uses pooled estimates from 15 prior ANDV investigations. We estimate the level of contact tracing and quarantine required for containment and quantify the consequences of incomplete or delayed intervention. Results We fitted the within-host-informed latent-time model to 34 cases and 33 reconstructed source- recipient pairs from the 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak in Argentina (Table 1; Figure 1). Transmission was concentrated near source symptom onset, with an estimated 42.4% of transmission events oc- curring before symptoms appeared (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%). The median transmission time was 0.07 days after source symptom onset (95% CrI: (-0.20) to 0.30 days), and the central 95% of transmission events occurred from 0.85 days before to 2.02 days after source symptom onset (Figure 1A). The median incubation period was 18.50 days (95% CrI: 16.50–19.50 days), with a central 95% distributional interval of 7.50–35.50 days (Figure 1C). An estimated 95% of infections developed symptoms by 31.50 days (95% CrI: 29.50–35.50), and 99% by 39.50 days (95% CrI: 35.50–44.50). The median generation interval was 22.50 days (95% CrI: 20.50–23.50 days) (Figure 1B), and the median serial interval was 21.79 days (95% CrI: 21.28–22.18 days) (Figure 1D). Thus, exposed individuals may require several weeks of follow-up even though onward transmission is concentrated within a narrow window around symptom onset. These estimates were broadly consistent with previous analyses of the Epuyén outbreak while providing model-based inference of latent infection times and transmission timing relative to symptom onset (Supplementary Results). Table 1: Estimated epidemiological characteristics of person-to-person ANDV trans- mission. Median estimates are reported with 95% credible intervals (CrIs), reflecting uncertainty in the estimated population median. The central 95% interval summarizes the expected range across individual infections or transmission events. Transmission timing is reported relative to source symptom onset, with negative values indicating transmission before symptom onset. Quantity Median estimate (95% CrI) Central 95% interval Incubation period 18.50 days (16.50–19.50) 7.50–35.50 days Latent period 13.50 days (10.50–15.50) 5.50–22.50 days Generation interval 22.50 days (20.50–23.50) 12.50–38.50 days Serial interval 21.79 days (21.28–22.18) 12.20–36.94 days Transmission timing (relative to symptom onset) 0.07 days (−0.20–0.30) −0.85–2.02 days 3 Figure 1: Estimated epidemiological timing distributions for person-to-person ANDV transmission. Panels show the inferred distributions of the (A) transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, (B) generation interval, (C) incubation period, and (D) serial interval. Solid curves represent posterior median densities, and shaded regions indicate the corresponding 95% credible intervals. Dashed vertical lines mark zero days. In panel A, negative values indicate transmission before source symptom onset; in panel D, negative values indicate that the recipient developed symptoms before the source case. To characterize the transmission conditions documented across settings, we analyzed 15 pub- lished ANDV investigations. A hierarchical negative-binomial model estimated a pooled reproduc- tion number of 0.24 (95% CrI: 0.12–0.48) and a shared dispersion parameter of 0.39 (95% CrI: 0.19–0.89), reflecting low average but highly variable realized transmission across this broader set of investigations. Together with the Epuyén-calibrated estimates (R=2.12, k=0.316), these results anchored an empirically informed range of ANDV transmission potential. Hereafter, we refer to simulations using the Epuyén and pooled parameterizations as the higher- and lower-transmission scenarios, respectively. The primary analysis reproduced the timing of the 2026 cruise-associated response, with inter- vention beginning on simulation day 35, 26 days after symptom onset in the first detected case. 4 We restricted the analysis to outbreaks that had reached at least two generations of transmission by then; this occurred in approximately 35% of higher-transmission simulations and 3% of lower- transmission simulations. Tracing failures had substantially greater consequences under higher transmission (Figure 2A). When tracing missed 5%, 10%, 25%, or 50% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts, post-response transmission outside quarantine occurred in 18.9%, 29.9%, 51.1%, and 70.8% of simulations, respectively. Under the lower transmission, this probability ranged from 0.7% with 5% missed to 7.8% with 50% missed. Among simulations with higher transmission and at least one additional post-response infection, missing 10% of contacts resulted in a median of 5 additional infections and a 95th percentile of 49. With 25% or 50% missed, the medians increased to 8 and 27, respectively, and the 95th percentiles to 111 and 351. With lower transmission, the median remained between one and two across tracing levels (Figure 2B). Quarantine burdens were substantially lower under lower transmission (Figure 2C). With 10% of contacts missed, the median number of retrospectively uninfected downstream contacts quaran- tined was 313 (IQR 185–440), compared with 1,821 (IQR 720–4,161) under the higher-transmission scenario. At lower transmission, the median burden fell by 49%, from 329 with complete tracing to 167 with 50% of contacts missed, because outbreaks were small and fewer contacts were traced. At higher transmission, fewer quarantines per case were offset by larger outbreaks and more tracing events, leaving the median comparatively stable but increasing the risk of very large quarantine burdens. Most response activity ended within the initial six-week quarantine period, but breakthrough transmission occasionally prolonged the response under the higher-transmission scenario. With 10% of contacts missed, the median additional response duration was zero months, the 95th percentile was 1.61 months, and 0.2% of simulations required at least four additional months of response activity. With 50% missed, the median increased to 1.02 months and the 95th percentile to 5.01 months. With lower transmission, additional response duration remained near zero (Figure 2D). The multinational response to the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak was initiated after seven confirmed or suspected cases were identified. To assess the consequences of delayed intervention, we initiated contact tracing and quarantine after different numbers of cases had been reported, assuming 95% tracing completeness (Figure 3). Under higher transmission, delaying intervention from the first to the twentieth reported case increased the probability of at least 100 infections from 2.7% to 38.2% and of at least 500 infections from 2.1% to 14.0%. Median outbreak size increased from 1 to 72 infections, median quarantine burden from 2 to 500 individuals, and the probability of quarantining at least 1,000 individuals from 2.7% to 36.0%. Under lower transmission, outbreaks rarely reached the later intervention points: only 13 of 10,000 simulations reached 10 reported cases, and none reached 20. Outcomes following greater delays therefore could not be estimated precisely. Under active containment, most simulated outbreaks ended before enough cases were detected to estimate the reproduction number precisely. Estimates from the first few detected cases were highly uncertain, with broad 95% credible intervals that commonly included R = 1 under both transmission scenarios (Supplementary Figure 5). Simulations assume 95% case detection, a gamma- distributed delay from symptom onset to detection with mean 2 days and SD 1 day, a gamma- distributed delay from detection to isolation with mean 0.5 days and SD 0.5 days, 99% effective isolation, and a fixed 42-day quarantine. However, the size of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak was much more probable under higher transmission: outbreaks of at least 13 cases occurred in 29.4% of higher-transmission simulations compared with 0.01% of lower- transmission simulations. Beyond final outbreak size, the observed timing of case accumulation was also poorly compatible with the pooled parameterization (pcompat = 0.0055). Nevertheless, this parameterization occasionally produced outbreaks of the observed magnitude. Simulations assumed 95% tracing completeness and varied the number of reported cases after which tracing and quarantine were initiated. Panels show the estimated distributions of (A) total infections and (B) individuals requiring quarantine under the higher-transmission (gray) and lower-transmission (black) scenarios across 10,000 stochastic simula- tions per transmission scenario and intervention delay. For each reported-case trigger, boxplots show the median, interquartile range, and 1.5× interquartile-range whiskers; points represent individual simulations beyond the whiskers. Outcomes were summarized among simulations that reached the specified reported-case trigger. The y-axes are shown on a logarithmic scale to visualize the highly right-skewed outcome distributions. The transmission scenarios were therefore difficult to distinguish from the first few detected cases: within-outbreak 95% credible intervals for R spanned 1 under both scenarios through 5 detected cases (Supplementary Figure 5). Lower-transmission outbreaks rarely reached more than 5 detected cases. This early uncertainty is compounded by the potential for transmission conditions to change as cases disperse into different settings. papers.title_zh: 人类 安第斯病毒 疫情的传播时机与遏制风险

analysis_zh.background: 2026年与阿根廷邮轮旅行相关的多国安第斯病毒(ANDV)疫情促使开展大规模接触者追踪和隔离,凸显了了解ANDV传播动力学及遏制效果的必要性。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究利用2018–2019年Epuyén疫情的传播配对数据,构建将病毒增殖、症状出现与传播关联的机制潜伏时间模型;在高传染性(R=2.12,k=0.316)和低传染性(R=0.24,k=0.39)情景下进行模拟,并在两代传播后实施干预。
analysis_zh.results: 估计有42.4%(95%可信区间18.2–69.7%)的传播发生在症状出现前,中位潜伏期为18.5天;在高传染性情景下,漏查10%接触者导致持续传播的概率为29.9%,且≥5,000人被隔离的概率为20.6%;而在低传染性情景下,持续传播概率低于8%。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果支持在大型国际暴露事件后迅速、全面开展接触者追踪和隔离,尽管成本高昂,可为ANDV的公共卫生应对策略提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 无法从首批检测病例精确估计后续传播风险,且提供的证据未报告样本量及具体宿主数据等关键细节。

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

analysis.background: In May 2026 an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, prompting public‑health actions; ANDV infections are usually sporadic and linked to rodent exposure, but clusters such as this occur.
analysis.methods: Using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic passenger, the authors infected golden Syrian hamsters and examined pathogenesis, tissue replication sites, innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified viral shedding.
analysis.results: The patient‑derived ANDV2026 was highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease; it induced a delayed type‑I IFN and inflammatory response, replicated in respiratory and extra‑respiratory tissues including brain; infected hamsters generated neutralising antibodies and T‑cell responses (mainly to L and N proteins); virus was shed via multiple routes and infectious aerosol was recovered, whereas a rodent‑derived control strain shed little and was aerosol‑negative.
analysis.contribution: The work confirms established ANDV pathogenic features and reveals previously undescribed airborne shedding, showing that phenotypic characterisation of outbreak isolates can aid preparedness, severity marker identification, and medical‑countermeasure development.
analysis.limitations: No explicit limitations are reported in the supplied evidence; results are derived from a hamster model and may not fully translate to human infection.

analysis.summary_en: Background: In May 2026 an HPS outbreak caused by Andes virus occurred on the MV Hondius, raising public‑health concerns; ANDV infections are usually sporadic and rodent‑linked but clusters happen. Methods: Researchers isolated ANDV from a presymptomatic passenger and infected golden Syrian hamsters, assessing pathogenesis, tissue tropism, immune responses, and shedding. Results: The patient‑derived ANDV2026 was highly pathogenic, causing severe lung disease, delayed type‑I IFN, inflammation, replication in lung, brain and other organs, elicited neutralising antibodies and T‑cell responses (L and N proteins), and was shed via multiple routes including infectious aerosol, unlike a rodent‑derived control strain. Contribution: The study confirms known ANDV disease mechanisms and uncovers airborne shedding, highlighting the value of phenotypic characterisation of outbreak isolates for preparedness and countermeasure development. Limitations: No explicit limitations are reported; findings are based on a hamster model and may not fully extrapolate to humans.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 来自 MV Hondius 爆发的病毒在仓鼠中高度致病并通过空气排出

analysis_zh.background: 2026年5月,在邮轮 MV Hondius 上检测到由 安第斯病毒(ANDV,安第斯病毒)引起的 汉坦病毒肺综合征 疫情,促使公共卫生行动;ANDV 感染通常为散发且与啮齿动物暴露相关,但此类聚集亦会发生。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用来自一名无症状乘客的 ANDV 分离株,作者感染金叙利亚仓鼠,研究其致病机制、组织复制部位、先天和适应性免疫应答,并定量病毒排放。
analysis_zh.results: 患者来源的 ANDV2026 在仓鼠中高度致病,导致严重肺部疾病;它诱导延迟的 I 型干扰素和炎症反应,在呼吸道及呼吸道外组织包括脑中复制;感染的仓鼠产生中和抗体和 T 细胞应答(主要针对 L 蛋白和 N 蛋白);病毒通过多种途径排放,且可分离到有感染性的气溶胶,而鼠源对照株排放少且气溶胶检测为阴性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作确认了已知的 ANDV 致病特征,并揭示了此前未描述的空气传播排放,表明对疫情分离株进行表型表征可帮助提升防备、识别严重性标记以及开发医学对策。
analysis_zh.limitations: 提供的证据中未明确报告局限性;结果来源于仓鼠模型,可能无法完全外推至人类感染。

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.
